what_this_is: A ledger of check findings that are CORRECT, PERMANENT and IRREPARABLE, so
that a RED contract row still means 'action required by you, now'. A check
that is permanently red trains people to ignore red -- and the usual cure, a
suppression list, can hide a real failure. This is not that.
IT IS CONSUMED EXACTLY, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS:
* a FAIL that is not listed here            -> RED (regression)
* an entry here that matches no FAIL        -> RED (stale entry, OR the
checker went blind and
stopped seeing it)
* an entry on a code that HAS a remedy      -> RED (only EMPTY-MANIFEST
and UNPARSEABLE may be
pinned; those record no
binary at all, so no tool
can ever reconcile them)
* an entry past `expires_utc`               -> RED
* all FAILs pinned, irreparable, unexpired  -> exit 3, reported KNOWN
KNOWN IS NOT PASS. It prints its own row in the contract table, with the
reason and the expiry. The reverse-direction rule means this file doubles as
a liveness assertion on the checker: if the scan ever stops finding these
two files, it fails loudly instead of turning green.
Cleaning the referenced artifacts up (they are scratch working space, and a
disk-reclaim pass may well remove them) will turn this check RED until the
matching entry is deleted. That is deliberate: a two-line diff is the price
of an acknowledgement that cannot silently outlive its condition.
adding_an_entry: 1. Confirm the finding's code is in IRREPARABLE_CODES. If a tool can fix it,
fix it -- the ledger will refuse the entry anyway.
2. Copy the `id` verbatim from the checker's output (CODE:repo-relative-path).
Globs, directories and bare codes are not accepted: an entry pins ONE
finding on ONE file, so a different failure in the same file is still RED.
3. State why no tool can repair it, and what the human remedy is.
4. Set an expiry. An acknowledgement with no expiry is a permanent suppression.

entries.why_irreparable: Zero bytes. The manifest names no exe, no digest and no fingerprint, so there is nothing for any tool to reconcile against any binary -- unlike a legacy manifest, which at least names a path that can be re-read while the file survives.
